project_scope.note: The canonical website currently has Clematis anchors but not Aquilegia; teach the family mechanism through Clematis while preserving broader family variation.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Go to the flower center: look for numerous free stamens and one to many mostly free carpels on a superior ovary/receptacle, without a Rosaceae-style hypanthium.
family_diagnostics.floral_parts: Sepals are free and may be petaloid; petals may be present, modified, reduced, or absent.
family_diagnostics.local_clematis: Clematis has opposite divided leaves, no true petals, showy petaloid sepals, many free stamens/pistils, and aggregate achenes with persistent styles.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Common family fruits are aggregates of achenes or follicles.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Do not count showy flower parts as petals automatically; in Clematis the showy parts are sepals.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: whole plant → high-value structure → reproductive confirmation → tie-breaker
visual_lesson.intro: Clematis is a great way to learn that showy flower parts are not always petals—and that free stamens plus free carpels matter more than color.

steps.title: 1 · Start with the vine
steps.look_for: A climbing perennial with opposite divided leaves.
steps.why_it_matters: Opposite leaves are unusual within much of Ranunculaceae but characteristic of Clematis.

steps.title: 2 · Call the showy parts sepals
steps.look_for: Four thick red showy sepals forming the urn-shaped flower; true petals are absent.
steps.why_it_matters: This prevents one of the most common flower-part mistakes in Clematis.

steps.title: 3 · Look toward the center
steps.look_for: Many separate stamens surrounding multiple pistils rather than a fused ovary complex.
steps.why_it_matters: Numerous free stamens + mostly free carpels is the core Ranunculaceae reproductive pattern.

steps.title: 4 · Follow to the achene head
steps.look_for: Many dry one-seeded achenes, each with a long persistent style that can become feathery.
steps.why_it_matters: Fruit architecture distinguishes Ranunculaceae from capsule-forming poppies and many Rosaceae.

comparisons.title: Ranunculaceae vs Rosaceae
comparisons.rule: Both can have many stamens and free carpels. Rosaceae commonly has stipules plus a hypanthium; Ranunculaceae usually lacks both.

comparisons.title: Ranunculaceae vs Papaveraceae
comparisons.rule: Poppies commonly have caducous sepals, free petals and a syncarpous capsule; Ranunculaceae commonly keeps free carpels or aggregate fruits.

visual_lesson.caveat: The current visual lock is Clematis-heavy; Aquilegia should become the contrasting 'petals present and spurred' card once promoted with images.
